text:
<!--
  THE AGENT'S JOB DESCRIPTION — editable capability text, same as prompt.md.

  Everything below is sent to the agent as its first user message, so it is part of the
  skill you are optimizing: reword it, restructure it, add or remove guidance, change the
  interaction contract. This comment block is STRIPPED before the agent sees it.

  LOAD-BEARING PLACEHOLDERS — these are filled in per task and must SURVIVE any edit:
    {instruction} {spreadsheet_path} {spreadsheet_content} {instruction_type}
    {answer_position} {output_path}
  Optional: {max_turns}. No other {braces} are allowed.

  If a required placeholder goes missing, or an unknown one appears, the candidate is
  REJECTED before any task runs — the agent would otherwise be told to write its answer to
  a path it was never given. A literal brace must be doubled: {{ or }}.
-->
You need to solve the following spreadsheet manipulation question. It contains six pieces of information:
- instruction: the question about spreadsheet manipulation.
- spreadsheet_path: the path of the spreadsheet file you need to manipulate.
- spreadsheet_content: the target range's total size, the location of the other graded copies
  of this workbook, each sheet's real data extent, and the first few rows of the content.
- instruction_type: Cell-Level Manipulation (answer_position is exact cell(s)) or Sheet-Level Manipulation (answer_position is the maximum range you may modify).
- answer_position: the cell(s)/range you must modify or fill in.
- output_path: write the modified spreadsheet file to this exact path.

### instruction
{instruction}

### spreadsheet_path
{spreadsheet_path}

### spreadsheet_content
{spreadsheet_content}

### instruction_type
{instruction_type}

### answer_position
{answer_position}

### output_path
{output_path}

### how your answer is graded (read before writing code)
Your FINAL code block is re-run UNCHANGED on three copies of this workbook whose data
differs; each output is graded cell-by-cell against a reference answer, comparing BOTH the
value AND the type. Only copy 1 is previewed above; the other two copies are already on disk
(paths in spreadsheet_content). Read and write using the exact spreadsheet_path and
output_path strings given above — the re-run substitutes the filenames — so never glob for
files or build paths from a copy number. In an EARLY turn you may open all three input copies
to confirm your logic generalizes; the final block itself must read only the one
spreadsheet_path.

Formulas are graded by their RECALCULATED value, not their formula text. Before grading, the
file is recalculated with headless LibreOffice, then each cell's resulting value and type are
compared:
- A plain cell formula (=IF(...), =INDEX(...), =SUMIFS(...), =VLOOKUP(...), =SUMPRODUCT(...),
  =WORKDAY(...)) recalculates correctly — keep it when the answer must track per-copy data.
  But confirm the value it will RECALCULATE to, not merely that the text was written.
- These do NOT reliably recalculate headlessly and grade as blank/stale: array/CSE formulas
  (openpyxl ArrayFormula), dynamic-array functions (UNIQUE/FILTER/SORT), TEXTJOIN, AGGREGATE,
  and any formula whose inputs are volatile (RAND/RANDBETWEEN/NOW/TODAY, directly or
  transitively). For these, compute the answer in Python and write the LITERAL result (a real
  number / str / bool / datetime) instead of the live formula.
- A formula that evaluates to "" writes a BLANK cell and lowers coverage — if a cell must be
  filled, make sure your result is a real value, not an empty string.

Reuse the answer pattern the workbook already shows:
- If cells inside or adjacent to the target range already hold the intended formula or label
  pattern (or the same formula is visible on another copy of this workbook), reproduce that
  SAME formula/criteria across the whole target range — do not invent a different variant, and
  do not add extra conditions (an extra date bound, filter, or divisor) the existing formula
  does not have.
- EXCEPTION: when the instruction says the existing formula is broken/wrong and asks you to fix
  it, correct it as instructed and compute the intended result from the raw source — do not
  reproduce the broken version or its stale cached value.
- If the workbook already computes the SAME statistic in adjacent or helper/summary cells (e.g.
  a COUNTIF/COUNTIFS/SUMIFS column, or a per-row total the sheet already derives), obtain your
  answer by referencing or replicating THAT formula rather than re-counting the raw cells in
  Python. Python string/number comparison diverges from Excel's (case sensitivity, surrounding
  spaces, text-vs-number equality, wildcards), so a parallel hand-rolled recount produces
  different totals than the reference, which was built from the sheet's own formulas.

Match the expected TYPE and format of each answer cell:
- If the target range already contains a worked-example cell, replicate its exact per-column
  type and formatting — text stays text, a real date stays a date, a number stays a number —
  and preserve any leading/trailing spaces the source keeps (do not strip them).
- When your answer value is looked up or copied unchanged from another cell, give it that
  source cell's own value AND python type — do not coerce a number into text or text into a
  number/date, and never leave an unresolved "=..." formula string in an answer cell.
- When you SPLIT or EXTRACT a piece out of a text cell, keep that piece as the original text
  (str), preserving its spacing — do not parse the piece into a date or number. This holds even
  when a pre-filled example cell in the range already HOLDS a real datetime/number value (not
  merely a date number_format): for a split/extract, the operation dictates the output type, not
  the example cell's stored type — every extracted piece stays a str.
- When the instruction asks you to CONVERT or STANDARDIZE a whole value into a date/time/number
  (e.g. "reformat as dd/mm/yy"), store a real datetime/number and set the cell's number_format
  to the requested display pattern — the pattern describes how the cell should DISPLAY, not a
  text string to write.
- If the instruction names the form a result may take (e.g. "the result may be #N/A" or the
  "output result may be '-'"), write that exact literal for those cases, not a numeric
  placeholder such as 0. Conversely, write a computed value in EVERY target cell the
  instruction expects to hold a real result — do NOT invent #N/A, "-", 0, or a blank for those
  cells; use such a placeholder only when the instruction explicitly says the result may take
  that form.
- When you match rows by a text key (a name, title, or code) to look up or join values,
  normalize BOTH sides the same way before comparing: trim surrounding whitespace including
  non-breaking spaces (\xa0), collapse internal double spaces, and unify curly/smart quotes and
  apostrophes to straight ones (’→', “”→"). A key that still fails to match after normalizing is
  NOT a licence to emit #N/A/"-"/blank — re-check the key extraction, because most apparent "no
  match" cases are a cosmetic difference and the reference resolves them to a real value.
- Rich-text and conditional-formatting cells are themselves the graded answer — preserve the
  CellRichText / cell formatting, and never flatten them to a plain string.

Fill exactly what is asked and nothing more:
- Fill every cell the instruction requires; add no extra labels, totals, headers, or summary
  rows it didn't request.
- For formatting or conditional-formatting tasks, keep the existing cell values and formulas
  unchanged and modify only the formatting.

You have up to {max_turns} rounds of interaction. In each round, reply with exactly ONE python code block:
1. Information-gathering code (e.g. inspecting the file, or all three input copies) — the execution result is returned to you.
2. Solution code that writes the modified file to output_path.
3. Verification code: re-open output_path and print, for each cell in answer_position, its
   value and its python type. Confirm ALL of the following; if any fails, fix your code and
   write again:
   a. Every cell the task requires is filled with the intended value, no cell you meant to fill
      is unexpectedly None, and a rich-text or formatting answer keeps its special type (not a
      plain string).
   b. If any answer cell holds a formula that may not recalculate headlessly (array/CSE,
      UNIQUE/FILTER/SORT, TEXTJOIN, AGGREGATE, or volatile inputs), recompute its result in
      Python and write that literal instead — do not trust the printed formula text as proof.
   c. Reproduce EVERY worked example, on EVERY copy — not just the previewed one. If the target
      cells (or an adjacent example) are already pre-filled with answer values in ANY of the
      three copies on disk, run your logic on EACH such copy and confirm it reproduces that
      copy's values exactly. An interpretation that fits copy 1 but not copies 2/3 is the WRONG
      rule — keep revising the logic until it reproduces all of them (do not copy the pre-filled
      values; recompute them). Matching only the previewed copy is the single most common way a
      task passes 1/3 and fails the rest.
   d. Coverage: no cell the instruction expects to hold a value may be left None or "". If a
      formula could evaluate to "" for such a cell (e.g. an outer IF(...,"")), that is a bug —
      return the real value instead. (Do not fill cells the pattern leaves intentionally blank.)
Reply without a code block when you are satisfied the saved file is correct.
If your code raises an error, the traceback will be returned to you; fix the code and try again.
